title: The rise of the second-hand economy
text:
Not so long ago, buying second-hand clothes carried a certain {1}. Today, resale apps have turned it into something close to a status symbol. What began as a niche hobby for bargain hunters has since {2} off, and the market is now worth billions, which has forced traditional retailers to {3} notice.

Part of the appeal is financial. With living costs rising, shoppers are understandably reluctant to pay full price for items that {4} value the moment they leave the shop. But money is not the whole story. Younger consumers in particular are increasingly aware of the environmental {5} of fast fashion, and many say that extending the life of a garment gives them the sense that they are doing their bit.

Sellers, too, have their reasons. Clearing out a wardrobe and making a little money on the {6} is hard to resist, especially when an app does most of the work. Some have even turned a casual pastime into a profitable sideline, carefully studying which brands {7} the highest prices.

Not everyone is convinced, however. Critics argue that resale platforms simply encourage people to buy more, safe in the {8} that they can sell their purchases on later. Whether the trend reflects a genuine shift in attitudes or merely a new form of consumption remains to be seen.

items.hint: Which noun naturally follows 'carry a certain…' to describe a negative social image?
items.explanation: We say something 'carries a stigma' (a negative social image). 'Shame' and 'disgrace' describe feelings or events, not something an activity 'carries'; 'scandal' is a public event.

items.hint: Think of a phrasal verb that means 'suddenly became very successful'.
items.explanation: 'Take off' means to become successful or popular very quickly. 'Set off' means to start a journey, and 'come off' is used for plans that succeed, not for a market that grows.

items.hint: Which verb completes the expression meaning 'to start paying attention'?
items.explanation: 'Take notice' means to start paying attention. We 'pay attention', not 'pay notice', and 'give notice' means to announce that you are leaving a job or a home.

items.hint: Look at what comes directly after the gap: only one verb can take 'value' as a direct object.
items.explanation: Things 'lose value'. 'Drop', 'fall' and 'sink' need the preposition 'in' ('fall in value'), which is not in the text.

items.hint: Only one of these words can describe damage or a disadvantage, not just money paid.
items.explanation: 'The environmental cost' is the harm something causes. 'Fee', 'charge' and 'fare' are only sums of money paid for a service or journey.

items.hint: Which expression means 'in addition to your main job or income'?
items.explanation: 'On the side' means as an extra source of income. 'On the spot' means immediately, and 'on the edge' and 'on the top' do not fit the meaning.

items.hint: Which verb is used when something is sold for a particular price?
items.explanation: Goods 'fetch' a price when they are sold. People 'earn' money, but a brand or item does not 'earn' or 'win' a price.

items.hint: Complete the fixed phrase 'safe in the …' meaning 'confident because you know something'.
items.explanation: 'Safe in the knowledge that…' is a fixed phrase meaning feeling confident because you know something. The other nouns do not combine with 'safe in the'.

title: Why we put things off
text:
Most of us know the feeling: a deadline is approaching, yet {1} of getting down to work, we find ourselves tidying the desk or scrolling through our phones. For a long time, procrastination was dismissed as a simple matter of laziness. Psychologists now believe that it has far more to do {2} managing emotions than managing time.

According to this view, we delay a task not because we are unwilling to work, but because the task itself makes us feel anxious, bored or inadequate. Putting it off brings instant relief, {3} is precisely why the habit is so hard to break. The trouble is that the relief is short-lived; {4} longer we wait, the worse we tend to feel.

So what can be done? One surprisingly effective strategy is to make the first step so small that it seems almost ridiculous. Rather than promising to write an entire essay, you might commit to writing {5} more than a single sentence. Once you have started, the task often turns out to be less daunting than it appeared.

It also helps to be kinder to yourself. Studies suggest that students who forgave {6} for procrastinating before one exam were less likely to do so before the next. Harsh self-criticism, it {7} out, only adds to the negative feelings that caused the delay in the {8} place.

items.hint: You need the first word of a two-word preposition meaning 'in place of'.
items.explanation: 'Instead of + -ing' means 'in place of doing something': instead of getting down to work, we do something else.

items.hint: Complete the expression 'to have something to do … something'.
items.explanation: 'To have (a lot / far more) to do with' means to be connected with. The preposition is always 'with'.

items.hint: You need a relative pronoun that refers back to the whole previous clause.
items.explanation: After a comma, 'which' can refer to a whole clause: 'Putting it off brings instant relief, which is why…'. 'That' cannot be used after a comma in this way.

items.hint: Look at the second half of the sentence: 'the worse we tend to feel'.
items.explanation: The double comparative structure is 'the + comparative…, the + comparative…': the longer we wait, the worse we feel.

items.hint: Which word before 'more than' means 'only'?
items.explanation: 'No more than' (or 'nothing more than') means 'only': you commit to writing just one sentence.

items.hint: Who did the students forgive?
items.explanation: The students forgave themselves, so we need the reflexive pronoun for 'students': 'themselves'.

items.hint: Which verb forms a phrasal verb with 'out' meaning 'is discovered to be the case'?
items.explanation: 'It turns out' means 'it has been discovered that'. It is often used as a comment in the middle of a sentence.

items.hint: Complete the fixed phrase 'in the … place', meaning 'originally'.
items.explanation: 'In the first place' means 'originally, at the beginning': the negative feelings caused the delay to begin with.

title: Football by numbers
text:
Twenty years ago, the idea that a spreadsheet might influence who played on a Saturday afternoon would have struck most managers as frankly {1}. Today, however, data analysts are an {2} part of almost every professional club, working alongside coaches and medical staff.

Clubs now record every pass, sprint and tackle, and the sheer {3} of information can be overwhelming. The real skill lies not in gathering numbers but in their {4}. A striker who rarely scores might, on closer inspection, turn out to be remarkably {5} at creating chances for his team-mates. Similarly, a midfielder whose {6} is regularly questioned by fans may in fact be covering more ground than anyone else on the pitch.

Not everyone welcomes these developments. Some traditionalists remain deeply {7} of any approach that reduces the beautiful game to a set of statistics. Qualities such as leadership and determination, they argue, are by their very nature {8}, and no algorithm will ever capture what happens in a dressing room at half-time.

items.hint: You need an adjective, and the idea seemed impossible to managers.
items.explanation: 'Struck someone as + adjective': the idea seemed impossible, so we need the negative adjective 'unbelievable' (un- + believe + -able).

items.hint: An adjective after 'an': analysts are now impossible to remove from clubs.
items.explanation: 'An inseparable part' means a part that cannot be separated. Note the negative prefix 'in-' and the suffix '-able' (not '-ible').

items.hint: After 'the sheer …' you need a noun.
items.explanation: 'The sheer abundance of' means the very large quantity of. The adjective 'abundant' becomes the noun 'abundance'.

items.hint: After 'their' you need a noun.
items.explanation: The skill lies in the 'interpretation' of the numbers: verb 'interpret' + noun suffix '-ation'.

items.hint: After 'remarkably' you need an adjective that is followed by 'at'.
items.explanation: 'Effective at doing something' means successful at it. 'Effect' (noun) becomes the adjective 'effective'.

items.hint: After 'whose' you need a noun: fans doubt how hard he tries.
items.explanation: 'Commitment' is the noun from 'commit': fans question how dedicated the player is. Remember: one 't' before '-ment'.

items.hint: An adjective followed by 'of', meaning 'not trusting'.
items.explanation: 'Distrustful of' (or 'mistrustful of') means not trusting something. You need both a negative prefix and the suffix '-ful'.

items.hint: An adjective: these qualities cannot be measured.
items.explanation: 'Immeasurable' means impossible to measure: negative prefix 'im-' + 'measure' + '-able'.

items.first: I didn't realise how expensive living in London was until I moved there.
items.after: to London that I realised how expensive living there was.
items.hint: Use a cleft sentence: 'It was only when…'.
items.explanation: 'It was only when + past simple + that…' is a cleft sentence that emphasises the moment you understood something. It replaces 'not… until'.

items.first: People say that the new coach has completely changed the team's attitude.
items.hint: Passive reporting structure: subject + is said + to-infinitive. Which infinitive refers to the past?
items.explanation: With passive reporting verbs we use 'is said + to have + past participle' when the action happened before the moment of speaking.

items.first: I regret not starting to save money when I got my first job.
items.after: saving money when I got my first job.
items.hint: A regret about the past needs 'wish' + past perfect.
items.explanation: To express regret about the past we use 'wish + past perfect': I wish I had started saving. 'I'd' counts as two words.

items.first: It's pointless trying to persuade Marta to support a different team.
items.after: to persuade Marta to support a different team.
items.hint: Use the expression 'There is no point (in) + -ing'.
items.explanation: 'There is no point (in) doing something' means it is useless to do it. 'In' is optional, and the verb after it takes the -ing form.

items.first: The match was cancelled because of the heavy snow.
items.before: The heavy snow meant that the match
items.hint: Which phrasal verb with 'call' means 'cancel'? Keep the passive.
items.explanation: 'Call off' means 'cancel'. The match did not cancel itself, so we need the passive: 'was called off' (or 'had to be called off').

items.first: As soon as the referee blew the whistle, the fans invaded the pitch.
items.after: the whistle than the fans invaded the pitch.
items.hint: 'No sooner' at the start of a sentence needs inversion with the past perfect.
items.explanation: 'No sooner had + subject + past participle… than…' means 'as soon as'. After 'No sooner' the auxiliary comes before the subject.

title: The immersion myth
text:
Ask anyone how to learn a language properly and the answer is almost always the same: go and live where it is spoken. The advice is so widespread that it has acquired the status of common sense. Pack your bags, the thinking goes, and the language will simply seep in, absorbed through conversations in cafés, overheard arguments on buses and the daily business of getting by. As someone who has spent twenty years studying how adults acquire second languages, I have come to regard this picture with a certain amount of suspicion.

Let me be clear: I am not arguing that spending time abroad is a waste. Some of my most rewarding moments as a learner happened far from home. My point is rather that immersion, on its own, guarantees remarkably little. I have met people who have lived in a country for a decade and still struggle to order a meal, and others who reached an impressive level without ever leaving their home town. Whatever separates the two groups, it is not their postcode.

What, then, makes the difference? The research points, perhaps unsurprisingly, to what learners actually do with the opportunities around them. Being surrounded by a language is not the same as engaging with it. Many students who go abroad end up spending most of their free time with people from their own country, speaking their own language and consuming the same media they would at home. They return with wonderful memories and a handful of useful phrases, but their grammar is largely unchanged. In a sense, they have been abroad without ever quite arriving.

There is also the question of what kind of input learners receive. Natural conversation is fast, messy and full of shortcuts. For a beginner, it can be little more than noise. Without some way of making sense of it, whether a teacher, a textbook or a patient friend, much of it simply washes over them. Paradoxically, the learners who benefit most from immersion tend to be those who arrive with a solid foundation already in place. They have enough of the language to notice what they are hearing, and noticing, as a growing body of evidence suggests, is where learning begins.

None of this would matter much if the immersion myth were harmless. But it is not. It encourages people to believe that progress is a passive process, something that will happen to them rather than something they have to work at. When the expected breakthrough fails to materialise, they conclude that they lack some mysterious talent for languages. I have lost count of the students who have told me, with genuine sadness, that they are just not good at languages, when the real problem was that nobody had shown them how to learn.

So what would I recommend instead? Go abroad by all means, but go with a plan. Set yourself small, specific goals: to have one conversation a day that lasts longer than five minutes, to read a local newspaper before breakfast, to keep a notebook of expressions you hear but do not yet use. Seek out situations that push you slightly beyond your comfort zone. And keep studying in a structured way, because the classroom and the street are not rivals; each makes the other more useful.

Perhaps the most valuable thing immersion offers is not the language itself but the motivation that comes from needing it. There is nothing quite like the frustration of failing to make yourself understood to send you back to your grammar book with renewed determination. Used well, that frustration is fuel. Left alone, it is merely discouraging.

items.question: In the first paragraph, the writer suggests that the advice to live abroad

options.A: has been proved correct by research.
options.B: is mainly given by language teachers.
options.D: underestimates how difficult moving abroad is.

items.evidence: it has acquired the status of common sense
items.hint: What does it mean when an idea becomes 'common sense'?
items.explanation: If advice has 'the status of common sense', people accept it automatically without examining it, which is why the writer treats it 'with suspicion'. Research (A) is not mentioned in this paragraph.

items.question: What point does the writer make in the second paragraph?

options.A: Time spent abroad is rarely enjoyable for language learners.
options.B: Where a person lives is not what determines their success.
options.C: People who stay at home usually learn languages faster.
options.D: It takes at least ten years to master a language abroad.

items.evidence: Whatever separates the two groups, it is not their postcode
items.hint: Look at the last sentence of the paragraph: what is a 'postcode' standing for?
items.explanation: 'Postcode' stands for where someone lives: location does not explain the difference between successful and unsuccessful learners. The writer says some people learned well at home, but not that this is usually faster (C).

items.question: What does the writer mean by saying that some students 'have been abroad without ever quite arriving'?

options.A: They found it hard to adapt to the local culture.
options.B: Their stay was too short to make any real progress.
options.C: They spent most of their time travelling rather than studying.
options.D: They did not really engage with the language around them.

items.evidence: end up spending most of their free time with people from their own country
items.hint: Read the sentences just before the phrase: who do these students spend their time with?
items.explanation: These students stay in a bubble of their own language and media, so they never really engage with the new language. Culture (A) and travelling (C) are not the point being made.

items.question: According to the fourth paragraph, which learners gain most from immersion?

options.A: those who already know a fair amount of the language
options.B: those who avoid textbooks and learn from conversation
options.C: those who are exposed to the fastest natural speech
options.D: those who have a patient friend to practise with

items.evidence: the learners who benefit most from immersion tend to be those who arrive with a solid foundation already in place
items.hint: Find the word 'Paradoxically' and read what follows.
items.explanation: A 'solid foundation' means they already know a good deal of the language. A patient friend (D) is mentioned only as one way of making sense of input, not as what makes learners benefit most.

items.question: Why does the writer believe the immersion myth is harmful?

options.A: It makes studying abroad more expensive than necessary.
options.B: It leads learners to blame their lack of progress on a lack of ability.
options.C: It discourages teachers from using structured methods.
options.D: It persuades students to give up their studies at home.

items.evidence: they conclude that they lack some mysterious talent for languages
items.hint: What do learners conclude when the breakthrough does not happen?
items.explanation: When progress does not come, learners decide they have no talent ('just not good at languages'), when the real problem is how they learn. Cost (A) and teachers' methods (C) are not mentioned.

items.question: In the final paragraph, the writer describes frustration as something that

options.A: should be avoided as far as possible.
options.B: usually disappears once a learner has a plan.
options.C: can be a positive force if it is used properly.
options.D: is a sign that a learner is not ready to go abroad.

items.evidence: Used well, that frustration is fuel.
items.hint: What is 'fuel' used for?
items.explanation: Calling frustration 'fuel' means it can drive you forward, but only if it is 'used well'; left alone it is just discouraging. The writer does not say it should be avoided (A).

title: AI in the lecture theatre
topic: students using AI tools in assessed work
intro: Four academics comment on whether university students should be allowed to use AI tools in assessed work.

texts.author: Helen Marsh, education researcher
texts.text: There is little doubt in my mind that relying on AI to draft essays deprives students of the very skills a degree is supposed to develop. Writing is not simply a way of displaying what we know; it is how we work out what we think, and a student who outsources that struggle loses something that cannot easily be recovered. Some colleagues place their faith in detection software, but I have seen too many honest students wrongly accused to share their confidence. Instead, I would move a greater share of assessment into the room: short oral examinations and supervised writing tasks reveal far more about a student's understanding than any take-home essay. I am also uneasy about the suggestion that universities should simply hand out premium AI subscriptions to everyone; that seems to me to solve the wrong problem.

texts.author: Daniel Okafor, computer scientist
texts.text: Banning AI tools from assessed work strikes me as both futile and short-sighted. Futile, because no current software can tell with any certainty whether a piece of text was produced by a machine; short-sighted, because graduates will be expected to use these tools throughout their careers. Used critically, AI can actually sharpen students' thinking: asking it for counter-arguments, or spotting its frequent mistakes, demands precisely the kind of judgement we claim to value. The real challenge is to design coursework in which students are open about how they have used AI and are marked on the quality of their reasoning. Universities must also accept responsibility for access. If the best tools are available only to those who can pay for them, we will simply have created a new form of inequality, so institutions should provide them to every student.

texts.author: Priya Nair, philosopher
texts.text: I find the current enthusiasm for AI in higher education worrying. Students who let software organise their arguments for them may produce polished work, but they are not learning to think independently, and that, surely, is what universities are for. Fortunately, the situation is not as hopeless as some claim. The latest detection systems, used alongside a tutor's knowledge of a student's previous work, identify machine-generated essays with considerable accuracy, and clear rules backed by consistent enforcement are entirely realistic. I therefore see no need to abandon the take-home essay, which remains one of the best ways of assessing extended reasoning. What we need is not a revolution in assessment but the courage to apply the rules we already have.

texts.author: Tom Reilly, linguist
texts.text: Much of the anxiety about AI seems to me misplaced. In my experience, students who learn to question what a chatbot tells them become more, not less, discerning readers, and that skill will serve them well. Where I part company with some enthusiasts is on coursework. Since nobody can reliably prove that a text was written by a machine, take-home essays have lost much of their value as evidence of individual achievement, and I would return the most important assessments to the examination hall, pen and paper included. None of this means students should be denied the tools outside exams. On the contrary, if access depends on whether a student can afford a subscription, universities have an obligation to step in and make those tools available to all.

items.question: Which writer shares writer A's view on the effect that using AI has on students' ability to think for themselves?
items.hint: Writer A thinks AI deprives students of skills. Who else sees AI as a threat to independent thinking?
items.explanation: C says students who let software organise their arguments 'are not learning to think independently', like A. B and D believe AI can sharpen thinking or make students more discerning.

items.question: Which writer has a different opinion from the others on whether AI-generated work can be reliably identified?
items.hint: Three writers doubt detection tools. Who trusts them?
items.explanation: C believes detection systems identify machine-generated essays 'with considerable accuracy'. A, B and D all say detection is unreliable.

items.question: Which writer expresses a similar view to writer B regarding the role universities should play in giving all students access to AI tools?
items.hint: B wants institutions to provide the tools to everyone. Who else talks about an obligation to provide access?
items.explanation: D says universities 'have an obligation to step in and make those tools available to all', like B. A is uneasy about handing out subscriptions, and C does not discuss access.

items.question: Which writer, like writer D, believes that the most important assessments should take place under supervised conditions?
items.hint: D wants exams in the examination hall. Who else wants assessment to happen 'in the room'?
items.explanation: A wants to move assessment 'into the room' with oral exams and supervised writing. B prefers open coursework and C wants to keep the take-home essay.

title: Lessons from a food truck
topic: a summer running a small business

paragraphs.text: Speed, unfortunately, was exactly what we lacked. Our van had been designed for selling ice cream, not for cooking, and the two of us kept getting in each other's way in the narrow space. Orders were forgotten, change was miscounted, and on one memorable occasion Leo poured a customer's chilli into the wrong container entirely.

One quiet afternoon she wandered over with a notebook and, without waiting to be asked, redesigned our entire operation. One person, she insisted, should take orders and money while the other did nothing but cook. The menu should be written above the hatch so that customers could decide before they reached the front. And the potatoes should be part-baked at home every morning.

The Rolling Spud, as the van was now called, had previously belonged to an ice-cream seller and still played a tinny version of a nursery rhyme whenever the engine started. It took us two days and most of our savings to remove the music box, and another week to persuade a mechanic that the brakes were worth saving.

These complaints, however, came mostly from the other stallholders rather than from customers. The organisers of the market eventually agreed to move us to a quieter corner, where the smell of frying potatoes would bother nobody, and the matter was quietly forgotten.

Our opening day, at a weekend market on the edge of town, was a disaster. We ran out of potatoes by eleven o'clock, burnt the chilli, and spent so long chatting to each customer that the queue stretched past the neighbouring stalls. By the end of the week, however, things had begun to improve.

By the time we sold the van at the end of the summer, we had paid back every penny we had borrowed and had enough left over to cover our rent for the autumn term. Leo, characteristically, wanted to celebrate by buying a second van.

Then August arrived, and with it the wettest fortnight anyone could remember. The weekend markets were cancelled one after another, and on the few days we did open, we sometimes sold fewer than twenty portions. Sitting in the van listening to the rain, we began to work out how much money we would lose if we sold it.

items.hint: The paragraph before ends with Leo having 'named' the van. Which paragraph mentions its name?
items.explanation: C begins 'The Rolling Spud, as the van was now called', which follows on directly from 'had already named it'.

items.hint: The next paragraph starts 'Those first few days…'. Which paragraph describes the first days of trading?
items.explanation: E describes the opening day and the rest of the first week, which 'Those first few days' then refers back to.

items.hint: The paragraph before ends by stressing the importance of speed.
items.explanation: A picks up the word 'speed' ('Speed, unfortunately, was exactly what we lacked'), and its problems explain why help is needed in the next paragraph ('Fortunately, help arrived').

items.hint: The next paragraph begins 'Her advice…'. Who gave advice?
items.explanation: B describes Marisol ('she') redesigning their operation, which is the 'advice' referred to in the following paragraph.

items.hint: The next paragraph mentions 'giving up' and 'the rain'.
items.explanation: G describes the rainy fortnight in August and the thought of selling the van, which explains 'That was the closest we came to giving up' and 'the rain also forced us…'.

items.hint: The last paragraph asks 'Would I do it again?'. Which paragraph describes the end of the summer?
items.explanation: F sums up the end of the summer and Leo wanting a second van, which leads naturally to the question 'Would I do it again?'. D does not fit anywhere: no complaints are mentioned in the text.

title: My first year in finance
topic: graduates describe their first jobs in finance
intro: Five recent graduates describe their first year working in finance.

sections.heading: Sara, analyst at an investment bank
sections.text: Nothing at university prepared me for the pace of my first few months. The hours were long, of course, as everyone warns you, but what really struck me was how little I seemed to know. My instinct was to keep quiet and work things out on my own, which in hindsight was a mistake: I spent whole evenings stuck on problems that a colleague could have solved in five minutes, simply because I didn't want to look foolish. The turning point came after my first big presentation. My manager took me aside and told me, quite bluntly, that my slides were cluttered and my conclusions were buried on page twelve. It stung at the time, but it was exactly what I needed to hear, and I still follow her rule of putting the answer first.

sections.heading: Tom, graduate trainee at an insurance company
sections.text: I joined on a two-year graduate scheme, which means I spend six months in each of four areas of the business. So far I have worked in claims and in pricing, and I am currently with the team that develops new products. Just as I start to feel comfortable, I move on and have to begin again, which keeps things fresh. The thing nobody mentioned during the interviews was how much of the job is writing. I assumed I would spend my days with numbers, but I produce reports, briefing notes and summaries for managers almost every day, often to tight deadlines. Each trainee is paired with a mentor from a different department, and mine has been a calm, encouraging presence, always ready to listen when I need to talk something through.

sections.heading: Aisha, risk analyst at a fintech start-up
sections.text: When I told my friends I was joining a company with twenty employees, several of them looked at me as if I had lost my mind. Most of them had accepted offers from large banks with impressive starting salaries, and I knew I was turning down rather more than I would be paid here. What tipped the balance was the chance to do real work from day one. Within my first week I was building the model that decides which customers we lend to, something a graduate at a big bank might wait years to be trusted with. It can be chaotic, since priorities change from one morning to the next, and I have taught myself to code in the evenings. But I would much rather be stretched than bored.

sections.heading: Pablo, auditor at an accounting firm
sections.text: Auditing has a reputation for being dull, and I won't pretend every day is thrilling. What makes it tough is that the firm expects you to qualify as a chartered accountant while doing the job, so for three years most of my weekends have gone on revision for one exam or another. The job itself takes me to a different client every few weeks, which I enjoy, although our arrival is not always greeted with enthusiasm. Finance directors know we are there to find their mistakes, and some make it very clear that they would rather we left as soon as possible. Working in small teams under pressure has taught me a great deal about getting on with people, even when everybody is tired and the deadline is the next morning.

sections.heading: Grace, financial adviser at a local firm
sections.text: I came into this job straight from a degree full of complex models, and my first meetings with clients were a disaster. I would launch into explanations of risk and diversification and watch their eyes glaze over. A pension or a mortgage is not an abstract problem for the people sitting across the table from me; it is their future, and many of them are anxious about it. So I have had to throw away the jargon and find ways of describing these ideas that anyone can follow, often with examples from everyday life. What I value most, though, is the sense of making a difference. When a couple tells me that they can finally afford to retire, or that their children's education is secure, I go home feeling that the work genuinely matters.

items.statement: I had to study for professional qualifications on top of my normal workload.
items.hint: Who mentions exams and weekends spent revising?
items.explanation: Pablo has to 'qualify as a chartered accountant while doing the job', revising at weekends.

items.statement: I was given considerable responsibility almost immediately.
items.hint: Who did 'real work from day one'?
items.explanation: Aisha was building the lending model 'within my first week', something others might wait years for.

items.statement: I wish I had been less reluctant to admit what I didn't know.
items.hint: Who kept quiet because they didn't want to look foolish?
items.explanation: Sara's instinct 'to keep quiet' instead of asking was, in hindsight, 'a mistake'.

items.statement: I have had to learn to explain technical ideas in plain language.

items.explanation: Grace had to 'throw away the jargon' and describe ideas 'that anyone can follow'.

items.statement: Some of the people I deal with at work are not pleased to see me.

items.explanation: Pablo says some finance directors 'would rather we left as soon as possible'.

items.explanation: Aisha was 'turning down rather more than I would be paid here'.

items.explanation: Sara's manager criticised her slides 'quite bluntly', and it was 'exactly what I needed to hear'.

items.statement: I was surprised by how much of my job involves producing written documents.
items.hint: Who says nobody mentioned the writing?
items.explanation: Tom had assumed he would work with numbers, but writes 'reports, briefing notes and summaries' almost every day.

items.statement: I find it rewarding to see the effect my work has on people's lives.
items.hint: Who talks about 'making a difference'?
items.explanation: Grace goes home 'feeling that the work genuinely matters' when clients can retire or pay for education.

items.statement: Regularly changing departments has kept the job interesting.
items.hint: Who moves to a new area every six months?
items.explanation: Tom spends six months in each area, and moving on 'keeps things fresh'.
